section_summary: This section comprises the State Department's docket index sheets (List of Papers) for file 894.00 covering 1930 through mid-1935, followed by the initial sequence of diplomatic despatches and memoranda from early 1930. The diplomatic reporting centers on the political maneuvering surrounding the dissolution of the Japanese Diet in January 1930 and the subsequent February 20 general election, which produced an absolute majority for Prime Minister Osachi Hamaguchi's Minseito party. It also includes an extensive survey of the fragmented Japanese proletarian political movement, tracing its ideological fissures, multi-member district electoral handicaps, and organizational lineages under universal manhood suffrage.

subfiles.about: A comprehensive State Department docket register listing incoming and outgoing despatches, telegrams, and cross-references regarding Japanese political affairs from January 1930 to mid-1935.
subfiles.summary: This cumulative docket index records documents 894.00/295 through 894.00/547, summarizing diplomatic correspondence and reporting on internal Japanese politics between January 1930 and June 1935. Entries chronicle major political developments, including the 1930 general elections, the shooting of Prime Minister Hamaguchi, the Manchurian Incident, the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai in the May 15 Incident of 1932, and the formation of successive non-party and coalition cabinets. The register notes the document number, sender, recipient, date, cross-reference decimal classifications, and brief purports for all papers filed under decimal file 894.00.
subfiles.title: List of Papers: Political Affairs - Japan (894.00/295 - 894.00/547)

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting the dissolution of the Japanese Diet on January 21, 1930, and analyzing party tactics and press reactions ahead of the February general election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Castle reports on the dissolution of the Lower House of the Imperial Diet on January 21, 1930, and the scheduling of a general election for February 20. The despatch details the Minseito government's tactical calculation to dissolve the Diet early while enjoying the positive momentum of lifting the gold embargo and superior electoral administration under Home Minister Kenzo Adachi. It reviews parliamentary interpellations by Seiyukai leader Tsuyoshi Inukai regarding naval ratios at the London Conference and minor ministerial corruption, contrasting them with the larger financial scandals plaguing the Seiyukai. Castle concludes with an analysis of divided editorial opinion across Tokyo newspapers and notes the organizational weaknesses of rival proletarian parties.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2: Dissolution of the Diet and Forthcoming General Election

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Telegram No. 32 regarding the decisive victory of the Japanese Government in the general election of February 20, 1930.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references confidential Telegram No. 32 sent from Tokyo on February 24, 1930, filed under 500.A 15 a 3/705. It records that the February 20 general election resulted in a decisive triumph for the Minseito government, which was now in a position to vigorously prosecute its foreign and domestic policies. The preliminary election returns recorded give the Minseito 273 seats, the Seiyukai 174 seats, and the remaining 19 seats scattered among minor parties and independents.
subfiles.title: Document File Note for Telegram No. 32 on General Election Returns

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch and genealogical chart analyzing the history, factional schisms, leadership, and electoral prospects of Japanese proletarian and labor parties.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Castle submits an extensive study of the Japanese proletarian political movement prior to the February 1930 general election, identifying chronic factional disunity as its primary vulnerability. The despatch surveys the evolution of labor organizations and political parties from 1925 onward, explaining how theoretical disputes, personal rivalries among leaders, and government suppression of radical elements led to fragmented groups including the Social Democratic Party, Japan Popular Party, New Labor-Farmer Party, National Popular Party, and Labor-Farmer Popular Party. Castle examines structural hurdles including the apathy of the working masses, traditional paternalistic household industrial relations, voter diffusion caused by rival proletarian candidates contesting the same multi-member districts, and chronic lack of campaign financing compared to major bourgeois parties. An attached genealogical chart traces the lineages and splits of the various labor and farmer parties leading up to 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 24: Developments in Japanese Proletarian Political Parties

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting the final distribution of seats in the Imperial Diet following the general election of February 20, 1930.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Castle confirms his earlier telegraphic report on the February 20 general election and transmits the final official breakdown of parliamentary seats in the Lower House. The governing Minseito won an absolute majority with 273 seats, while the opposition Seiyukai captured 174 seats. Minor party and independent representations comprised the Kokumin Doshikai (6), Kakushin Club (3), Neutrals (5), and Proletarians (5, divided among Shakai Minshuto, Nihon Taishuto, and Ronoto) for a total of 466 seats. The ambassador notes that a detailed analytical survey of the election is being prepared for dispatch in the next diplomatic pouch.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 43: Final Returns of the General Election of February 20, 1930

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum highlighting the key factors behind the Minseito election victory as presented in Ambassador Castle's Despatch No. 58.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Division analyst R. S. M. summarizes and comments upon Ambassador Castle's Despatch No. 58 regarding the February 1930 Japanese general election. The memorandum identifies Seiyukai corruption scandals, financial extravagance, and internal discord versus Premier Hamaguchi's personal integrity and Home Minister Adachi's skilful campaign management as the deciding factors. The author observes that high voter turnout exceeding eighty percent indicated growing political engagement, while the decline in independent and proletarian seats signaled a possible shift toward a two-party system, driven partly by contrasting economic philosophies of retrenchment versus positive spending.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Despatch No. 58 regarding the Japanese General Election

subfiles.about: Comprehensive analytical despatch detailing the causes, campaign management, electoral mechanics, and political significance of the Minseito's landslide general election victory.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Castle provides an in-depth survey explaining how the ruling Minseito achieved an absolute majority of 40 seats in the Lower House of the Diet. The despatch attributes the result to popular revulsion against Seiyukai corruption scandals—notably involving General Yamanashi, Heikichi Ogawa, and Jiro Amaoka—and excessive interference during the Tanaka ministry. Castle analyzes the brilliant electoral tactics of Home Minister Kenzo Adachi, who curtailed overt police interference, strictly suppressed opposition vote-buying, and achieved an equal distribution of votes among Minseito candidates under the intermediate multi-member electoral system. The report also highlights Prime Minister Osachi Hamaguchi's personal reputation for integrity, public confidence in his fiscal retrenchment and lifting of the gold embargo, and superior campaign financing.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 58: Detailed Survey of the Japanese General Election of February 20, 1930
